new_text: "Mama dislikes being disturbed in the evening," Eliza remarked. I soon rose, quietly removed my bonnet and gloves, uninvited, and said I would just step out to Bessie—who was, I imagined, in the kitchen—and ask her to find out whether Mrs. Reed was willing to see me tonight. I went, and having found Bessie and sent her on my errand, I took further steps. It had always been my habit to shrink from arrogance; received as I had been today, a year ago I would have resolved to leave Gateshead the very next morning. Now, it suddenly became clear to me that this would be foolish. I had come a hundred miles to see my aunt, and I must stay until she was better—or dead. As for her daughters' pride or folly, I must set it aside and make myself independent of it. So I spoke to the housekeeper, asked her to show me a room, told her I should probably be a visitor for a week or two, had my trunk taken to my room, and followed it there myself. I met Bessie on the landing.

new_text: I did not need to be shown to that well-known room, to which I had so often been summoned for punishment or scolding in the old days. I hurried ahead of Bessie; I softly opened the door. A shaded lamp stood on the table, for it was growing dark. There was the great four-poster bed with amber hangings, as before; there the dressing table, the armchair, and the footstool where I had been made to kneel a hundred times to beg pardon for sins I had not committed. I glanced into a certain corner nearby, half expecting to see the thin outline of a cane that used to lurk there, ready to leap out like an imp and sting my trembling palm or shrinking neck. I approached the bed; I drew back the curtains and leaned over the high-piled pillows.

new_text: I remembered Mrs. Reed's face well, and I eagerly looked for the familiar image. It is a good thing that time dampens the thirst for revenge and silences the promptings of rage and aversion. I had left this woman in bitterness and hate, and I came back to her now with no feeling except a kind of pity for her great suffering, and a strong desire to forget and forgive all wrongs—to be reconciled and join hands in friendship.

How often had it lowered on me with menace and hatred! And how the memories of childhood terrors and sorrows revived as I traced its harsh line now! And yet I bent down and kissed her. She looked at me.

new_text: I had once vowed never to call her aunt again; but I thought it no sin to forget and break that vow now. My fingers had found her hand where it lay outside the sheet. If she had pressed mine kindly, I would at that moment have felt real joy. But cold natures are not so easily softened, nor natural hatreds so quickly erased. Mrs. Reed pulled her hand away, and turning her face from me, remarked that the night was warm. Again she looked at me so icily that I knew at once her opinion of me—her feeling toward me—was unchanged and unchangeable. I could see by her stony eye—impervious to tenderness, unreachable by tears—that she was determined to consider me bad to the last; because to believe me good would give her no generous pleasure, only a sense of humiliation.

Her own fortune she had taken care to protect; and when her mother died—and it was very unlikely, she remarked calmly, that she would either recover or linger long—she would carry out a long-cherished plan: seek a retreat where strict habits would be permanently safe from disturbance, and place firm barriers between herself and the frivolous world. I asked if Georgiana would go with her.

new_text: The nurse came in, and Bessie followed. I stayed another half hour, hoping to see some sign of softening; but she gave none. She was sinking rapidly into stupor; her mind did not rally again. At midnight she died. I was not there to close her eyes, nor were either of her daughters. They came to tell us the next morning that it was over. By then she had been laid out. Eliza and I went to see her; Georgiana, who had burst into loud weeping, said she dared not go. There lay Sarah Reed's once robust and active body, rigid and still: her flint-like eye was shut beneath its cold lid; her brow and strong features still bore the stamp of her unyielding soul. A strange and solemn sight she was to me. I gazed at her with gloom and pain: nothing soft, nothing sweet, nothing pitying, or hopeful, or subduing did the spectacle inspire—only a grating anguish for her woes, not my loss, and a sombre, tearless dread at the fearfulness of death in such a form.

new_text: I knew there would be pleasure in seeing my master again, even though it was shadowed by the fear that he would soon cease to be my master, and by the knowledge that I was nothing to him. But there was always in Mr. Rochester (or so it seemed to me) such an abundance of the power to communicate happiness that to taste even the crumbs he scattered to stray and stranger birds like me was to feast richly. His last words were balm: they seemed to imply that it mattered to him whether I forgot him or not. And he had spoken of Thornfield as my home—if only it were!

new_text: That evening I firmly closed my eyes against the future. I stopped my ears against the voice that kept warning me of approaching separation and coming grief. When tea was over and Mrs. Fairfax had taken up her knitting, and I had settled in a low chair near her, and Adèle, kneeling on the carpet, had nestled close to me, and a sense of shared affection seemed to surround us with a ring of golden peace, I offered a silent prayer that we might not be parted far or soon. But when, as we sat like this, Mr. Rochester entered unannounced, and looking at us seemed to take pleasure in the sight of so harmonious a group—when he said he supposed the old lady was all right now that she had her adopted daughter back again, and added that he could see Adèle was "prête à croquer sa petite maman Anglaise"—ready to devour her little English mama—I half dared to hope that even after his marriage he might keep us together somewhere under the shelter of his protection, not entirely banished from the sunshine of his presence.
